02-bug-fixing.notes: Every implementation except G and K matches my reference model on get/put over 3000 random traces, so behavioural differences are almost entirely about expired-entry removal on get (G, K) and V's O(n) get. Regression coverage was scored by running each suite against 17 contract mutants (falsy check, wall-clock put, wall-clock put+get, > boundary, get without LRU refresh, get refreshes TTL, put-update keeps old timestamp, put-update keeps old value, put-update without recency, put-update evicts another entry, no purge, purge of LRU-front only, evict MRU, two variants each for max_size/ttl validation) built on a correct reference; for O and R (which pin len() excluding expired entries) a len-purging reference was used. The two most common gaps were (a) purge tests that put the expired entry at the LRU end, so plain LRU eviction passes them, and (b) update-at-capacity tests that update the LRU key, so the original popitem bug passes them. A get-does-not-delete mutant was ignored because the brief does not require removal. Suites that pin unspecified len() semantics (B, O, R) lost 0.25. Ties at 10 (J,M,Q,T,U,A) and at 9.75 are ordered arbitrarily. G versus P (both 9.25) was close: G has better tests but fails a hidden contract test. The brief is ambiguous on len() and on whether to purge below capacity, so S's lazy purge was not penalised.

All 26 compose files render with `docker compose config` when given a dummy .env. 04-project-maintenance.notes: Two facts drove most of the scores. (1) Our own probes confirm that LooseVersion.__str__ returns its input unchanged: a 35-input differential against real distutils on Python 3.11 matched an identity function on every non-empty string. So pass-through implementations (C, Q, V, M, H, G, E, A, D, L, O, P, R, W) preserve behaviour, while packaging-based or regex canonicalising ones (I, J, K, S, T, X, Y, Z, N, B, U, F) change output for spellings like 1.02, 2024.01.15, v1.2 and 1.0-rc1. (2) The fixture's flat layout (slugkit.py next to test_slugkit.py) makes setuptools refuse to build. We confirmed this with setuptools 84 build_wheel on a copy of each submission. Only C, E, G, H, I, K, M, N, Q, V and Z declared py-modules; every other submission's CI `pip install -e .` step fails on every matrix job. Close calls: Q vs V (both 9.5): Q ranks higher for its in-suite parity test against LooseVersion. C beats both on its ruff pin, format check and explicit diagnosis. M vs E (8.75): M is byte-for-byte faithful, while E invents a ValueError claim about LooseVersion. Z vs P (7.5): Z's CI and build actually work and its behaviour change is fully disclosed, whereas P preserves behaviour but left the build broken after diagnosing it. Ruff 0.16.1 was used for linting; all submissions pass the classic default rule set (E4,E7,E9,F). Ruff 0.16's expanded defaults flag SIM117/PLW1510 in some test files, which we did not hold against anyone. Not verified: real GitHub Actions runs and network-dependent installs. Process notes (F network attempt, K network installs, I no execution) were factored into communication. 'Could not run' statements were taken as honest where consistent.

It uses server-wins LWW on an opaque form_data JSON blob while claiming field-level merge, and treats base_version as idempotency. It misreads the 24h rule as an offline grace period: it blocks further local input on an unsynced inspection after 24h, which reintroduces the failure the brief is trying to remove. It backfills 90 days of assignments (more PII on device). Purge runs only on an accept event. A D2 'P2P ephemeral session' option is odd, and pilot gates include invented durations (2 weeks) and thresholds.

No decision milestone; invented numbers (5-10 inspectors, ≥98%, <10%, 2 weeks)

That move is flagged as a compliance decision (D1), but it reinterprets the brief's supervisor-review workflow. The residual risks are listed honestly.

Milestones M0-M8 have brief ACs, and M1 claims a reversible schema migration. Decisions are one-liners.

Purge runs at accepted_at+24h after the device learns of acceptance, and the plan never tackles a tablet that stays offline. The RESPONSE ranks offline auth above that gap. Same-field conflicts silently go to the supervisor with a toast. The pilot uses invented numbers (5-15 inspectors, 2 weeks, ≥95%, 30-minute cellular backlog).

App rollback via MDM 'preserves data (verify)'. Milestones M1-M8 have ACs but there is no decision gate.

muse-wonder.summary: A clear, well-reasoned plan with 10 assumptions (if-wrong and validate-by), 8 decisions with a Blocks column, and milestones M0-M6 with observable ACs. The conflict policy is sensible: auto-merge disjoint fields, keep both values for notes, manual choice for structured fields, never auto-apply pass/fail. Purge runs on learned acceptance plus overdue flagging, but there is no mechanism for a device that never learns of acceptance. The decision set is smaller than the top plans.

gpt-6-luna.summary: A concise plan with the acceptance-gated design: purge receipt before final acceptance, or an enforceable lease. It uses strict record-level conflicts resolved by the supervisor in a minimal web workflow. It has decision and decision-log tables and M0-M7 with clear ACs. It covers the required topics but with less depth (7 brief assumptions, no failure-path detail), and supervisor-only conflict resolution plus blocked acceptance carry product cost.

hy4-preview-codebuddy.summary: A strong, well-organized plan. It has an assumption table typed Verifiable/Load-bearing, an ownership matrix, invariants (e.g. never purge with a non-empty outbox), 12 decisions, and a milestone table with deps, ACs and critical path. The purge runs at accepted_at+24h rather than as soon as possible, and does not address a device that never learns of acceptance. Its quarantine path for unsynced accepted work keeps customer data past the deadline.

06-product-planning.notes: No objective checks beyond C's process note (chat interface, no tools); for a planning task that note does not change the grade. The main separator was the 24h purge: the best plans close the 'tablet never learns of acceptance' gap. R uses a cap anchored on the server's submission-receipt time; E, I and K purge at server-confirmed submission; D proposes a max-retention cap. L, S and Y gate acceptance on purge, which is compliant but operationally costly. Q redefines acceptance as the submit commit. The weaker plans purge only after learning of acceptance (A, F, G, J, M, T, U, V, W, Z) or misread the rule (O, P, X). Close calls: K/E/I tie at 9.25 (K ranked first for its residual-risk analysis and numbered ACs; E for its no-tablet-merge UX). H/D tie at 9.0. Q vs L at 8.75 (Q's field-level merge is more pragmatic than L's aggregate conflicts). C/Z/B/S tie at 8.25. Invented pilot sizes and durations were penalized under product judgment (A, F, O, P, U, X). I could not verify facts against a real codebase (none provided). The only executable check was C's DDL, which failed in sqlite3.

deepseek-v4-pro.summary: 'The Salt Archive': Mara finds a voicemail from herself telling her to stop archiving. The salt motif and the physical detail are competent. But the turn is spelled out in an essay paragraph, the humor is announced as humor, and the future message drifts into a quasi-supernatural 'the water wants you' register.
strengths: Salt motif carried through card reader, laptop fan, key and photograph (lines 17, 35, 43)
Mrs. Okafor opening scene is grounded and avoids weather exposition
weaknesses: Labels its own joke: 'The dry humor arrived, as it always did, at the worst moment' (line 33). That is a mechanical tick of the box, not subtext
The meaning change is explained outright: 'Here is what she understood... the message was not a warning from the future. It was a message she had not yet sent' (line 39)
The lockbox setup pays off with nothing (line 43), and 'The water... wants you to keep recording them' (line 25) edges toward the villain/supernatural register
Closing lines are generic: 'Some messages... were meant to be kept, and carried, and let go of, all at once'

It has striking lines and an ambitious idea (salt as a seal). But the logic is muddled, it moves the premise to eleven years, and RESPONSE.md breaks the sentence limit.

A coda ten years on shows the line was ordinary permission said at a bakery bench, not a farewell from someone beyond rescue. The prose is spare and grounded, the turn comes through scene rather than explanation, and the humor is light and well placed.

A tram's 'three blows, a space, another blow' and the new flat's number reframe it as settling into a new home. It is restrained and precise, with fully earned subtext. The butcher's unopened fourth message mirrors her own restraint (line 53)

Spectrum analysis and a notch filter reveal pine wind and Soren's cough, so the speaker is safe on the bluff. A permission.').

muse-wonder-full.summary: 'What the Salt Keeps': Mara's future voice says 'Don't send it. He comes anyway, and he brings the van... Mind your thumb.' After playing her own plea to Mara, she reinterprets the message as a job description. It has lovely touches, but the reversal is delivered in two long explanatory paragraphs.

Inventive motif turn: salt 'precipitating out of forty seconds of audio' (line 25)
'a timestamp could be an appointment' (line 39) is a strong closing idea

07-creative-writing.notes: All 26 STORY.md files fall inside 800-1,100 words by wc -w (K 1099, B/O 1098 and A 1096 are near the cap). Every story has a title, close third person, the salt motif and some humor, so constraint adherence mostly separates on stated premise/format facts: B (eleven years; 5-sentence RESPONSE), S (nine years four months), H (timestamp zeroed), W (dated today; explanatory 'quantum' monologue; weather-ish opening), K (heading in RESPONSE), and A and Q (jokes announced as 'dry humor'). The top tier (M, L, D, R) all carry the reversal through planted physical detail rather than explanation. M edges L and D on legibility: its clue chain ('love', fourth vs ninth rail, 'Set 20 fast') lands the reversal without a paragraph of decoding, while L and D are as subtle but riskier for a reader to miss. Several mid-tier entries (G, N, O, P, T, X) lose prose and payoff credit for decoding the message line by line in a 'Not a warning. A permission.' paragraph, a pattern common across the cohort. Room-tone reveals and a closing phone call recur often, which limited originality scores for P, I, T and Y. V and Y share a near-identical skeleton (froze over the gain knob, 'not a synthesized clone/model', release via the residents' files). Scored on the text only. Could not verify authorial intent behind ambiguities (C's cancelled recording, K's first playback lacking the restored clause). Judged these as minor logic snags.
